extracted.intended_audience: student journalists and reporters learning how to cover illnesses, deaths, obituaries, and special-event news
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for reporting news about illness, surgical operations, sudden death, obituaries, and related special-event items (also examples of reporting commencement and class-day events). Focuses on what to include, tone, and human-interest treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of 'Illness and Death' stories
rubrics_metrics.description: In this class of news stories are included those concerning the illness or death of persons known in the community or in the world at large, as well as those dealing with illness, surgical operations, and deaths that are sufficiently unusual to be matters of general interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this scope to decide what events belong in the category — prominent local figures, world-known persons, unusual surgical cases or deaths of general interest. The chapter groups surgical operations, sudden deaths, and human-interest illness items under this heading and illustrates each with examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primarily informative but allow human-interest development
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories of this kind are primarily informative in character, but the importance of the personal element permits effective human interest development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain factual, informative reporting as the backbone, while using personal detail (quotes, domestic setting, reactions) to deepen reader engagement. Balance hard facts (cause, dates, medical facts) with human context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pathetic (emotional) phases can add value
rubrics_metrics.description: Pathetic phases of illness or death sometimes give value to news that otherwise would be of slight interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek poignant, sympathetic elements (final words, devoted relatives, small personal habits) that make an otherwise minor item resonate. Use such elements to justify running or expanding a story, but avoid exploiting grief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seriousness demands dignity of treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: The seriousness of the subject demands dignity of treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid flippant, joking, sensational, or intrusive tones when covering illness and death. Respect privacy, use measured language, and present facts with decorum. The examples show restrained reporting of lonely deaths, veterans' funerals, and tragic sudden deaths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obituary purpose: beyond biographical facts
rubrics_metrics.description: In writing an obituary the purpose should be not only to give biographical facts but to bring out the significance of a personality. A well written obituary is a constructive interpretation of the meaning of a person's life and work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An obituary should combine essential biographical data (dates, offices, family, career milestones) with interpretation: why the person mattered, their character, contributions, and legacy. Use anecdotes and selected achievements to illuminate significance rather than merely listing facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsworthiness criterion: prominence and unusualness
rubrics_metrics.description: Include illness or death of persons known in the community or world at large, and deaths or surgical/medical cases that are sufficiently unusual to be matters of general interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use prominence (public figure, community leader) or the unusual character of the case (rare surgery, exceptional circumstances, or a dramatic last request) as thresholds for coverage. Examples: a veteran fireman’s long service and patent-holding; a conductor’s dying request to keep a punctual record; a unique heart operation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report surgical operations with procedure, outcome, and broader significance
rubrics_metrics.description: When surgical operations are reported, describe the operation and its outcome and indicate its medical or social significance (e.g., opening a new field in surgery or suggesting new possibilities for revival under anesthetics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include technical but comprehensible description of what was done, immediate results, experts' assessments, possible wider implications, and planned follow-up (tests, studies). Use authoritative quotes from physicians and note ethical/experimental follow-ups when relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use scene-setting, local color, and direct particulars to humanize illness accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: Human-interest illness pieces should use neighborhood detail, objects, actions, and direct speech to paint a vivid picture (e.g., closed shopfront, brown-paper curtains, a man wanting to die among his books).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open with arresting, concrete details that establish setting and sympathy (objects, diary entries, pets, neighbors’ reactions). Include small documentary elements (signs, diary lines) and quotes to authenticate and humanize the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report special occasions by recording names, roles, honors, statistics, and notable features
rubrics_metrics.description: Coverage of commencements, class day, exhibitions, and similar special occasions should include speakers, presiding officers, innovations in the program, attendance, costumes, awards, and class statistics (honors, averages, career intentions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give readers the who/what/when/where and the noteworthy specifics that characterize the event: names of speakers and honorees, unusual features (class costumes, new dinners), program highlights (fireworks, music), and interesting class data (height/weight/age averages, career plans). These details capture the flavor and importance of the occasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware that different outlets may frame the same incident differently
rubrics_metrics.description: The same incident may be reported very differently by different newspapers (e.g., a Chicago morning paper versus a New York evening paper), reflecting differences in tone, emphasis, and selective facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When preparing copy, consider audience and outlet conventions — tone, level of detail, local angle, and narrative emphasis will vary. Comparative examples in the text show variations in focus (anecdotal, humorous framing vs. straight biographical account); adapt accordingly while preserving accuracy.
